title: Annotation biases and probe habits — scratchpad
content:
Quick context:
- Sprint focus: why our lightweight probes / human labels drift over time and across labelers. Looking at annotation patterns from the last two evals (2026-09, 2026-10) we see consistent skew on 'partial credit' cases.
- Goal: produce a short bakeable experiment and a set of rubrics we can reuse across future probe sets. Want something that is cheap (<= 1000 judgments) and diagnostic for labeler bias vs model failure.

Notes / observations from raw data:
- Labeler A and B flagged the same set of outputs as "hallucination" but disagreed on severity: A used a binary tag, B used 3-tier severity. Aggregation masked that.
- We had a high correlation between longer context prompts and lower inter-annotator agreement. Hypothesis: more context increases ambiguity about "reference answer" (annotators apply different assumptions).
- Some instructions in the task UI nudged labelers toward conservative answers: phrase "only accept exact matches" appears in the UI copy used for one batch. That likely reduced partial-credit labels.

Concrete hypotheses to test:
H1: Instruction phrasing (binary vs graded examples) changes distribution of "correctness" labels enough to flip model ranking for subtle models.
H2: Warm-up calibration with 10 canonical examples increases inter-annotator agreement by ~10–15 percentage points.
H3: When prompt includes explicit retrieval context cue ("source: ..."), annotators give more weight to non-model evidence and are more likely to penalize hallucination.

Mini-experiments (cheap, run in next 2 weeks):
- A/B annotation UI copy (binary vs graded) with same model outputs, 200 examples each, 3 annotators per example. Measure: pairwise kappa, distribution shift, and whether top-1 model flips. (Owner: Julian)
- Warm-up calibration test: run 100 control vs 100 calibrated (10 warm-up examples + micro-feedback). Measure agreement and time-per-judgment. (Owner: Rina)
- Source-cue sensitivity: for a subset of retrieval-augmented outputs, show context vs hide context. See change in false-hallucination rate. (Owner: Maya)

Sketch of annotation rubric (working):
- Category (one-of): Correct, Partially-Correct, Incorrect, Not-Evaluable.
- Severity (if Incorrect): Minor / Major / Critical.
- Evidence tag: Reference present / Reference absent / Ambiguous.
- Confidence (1–5): how sure was the labeler.
- Free-text: 1–2 sentence justification (only for "Incorrect" or "Partial").

Aggregation plan:
- For model scoring use vector of (correctness_score, mean_confidence, proportion_evidence_present). Convert to scalar via weighted sum but keep the vector for diagnostics. Avoid simple majority for final ranking in small-N settings.

Open questions and todo:
- How to surface example-level disagreement quickly to model teams? Idea: small "disagreement dashboard" that surfaces top 50 examples by vote entropy with annotator justifications. (Spike: 1d prototype using existing spreadsheet exports)
- Should we preserve annotator metadata (seniority / training) in analysis? Pros: explains patterns. Cons: privacy + sampling bias. Talk to legal/product about PII.
- Explore bootstrapped confidence intervals for model rank when N judgments per example is small (n=3). Are we overconfident about ranking stability?

Implementation notes / tracking links:
- Baseline data CSV: /mnt/evals/2026-10/annotation-batch-v2.csv (ask SRE for access)
- Proposed small eval PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/mini-evals/pull/412 (has skeleton annotation UI changes)
- Slack thread: #evals "annotation drift" (refer to messages around Nov 1)

Short-term plan (this sprint):
- Week 1: wire A/B UI copy change into mini-evals PR, recruit 6 annotators, run 400 judgments. Quick analysis script to compute kappa and model-rank delta. (Owner: Julian)
- Week 2: run warm-up calibration test, build quick disagreement export and push to Confluence page with initial findings. (Owner: Rina)

Longer-term thoughts:
- Might be worth building a small "calibration lab" in Console where product teams can define a 10-example warm-up that becomes required before annotation starts. Standardize examples per domain (QA, summarization, code).
- Probabilistic label aggregation (bayesian) could give better uncertainty for small-N; talk to Applied ML for priors.

Loose references I want to re-read before finalizing rubric:
- CrowdTruth / annotator disagreement literature (classic) — summarize later
- "Measuring Agreement among Raters" primers (Fleiss, Krippendorff notes)
- Recent arXiv: annotation calibration for LLM evals (save list below when I dig it up)

Notes to self (quick reminders):
- Keep prompts minimal when comparing models — extra scaffolding in prompt changes human interpretation.
- Preserve the free-text justifications for a small sample (10%) and do manual thematic analysis.
- When reporting rank deltas, show bootstrap CI and sample size.

Unread items / reading queue (pull these into formal lit list later):
- paper: "When Humans Disagree: Calibration and Aggregation in ML" (placeholder arXiv link)
- blog: "How micro-instructions shape annotations" (internal blog, @Maya wrote draft)

If time: sketch a lightweight experiment that asks annotators to label 'why' they marked incorrect (select from short list) instead of free-text — likely faster and more structured for analysis.

End scratchpad. Keep this file minimal and evolve to a proper PRD once we have pilot results.
